parsing_res_list.block_content: ## 4 Main Result
The answer to the question of the previous section turns out to be positive.
For an affine hyperplane  $ H \subset \mathbb{R}^n $ set
$$ U_{\varepsilon}(H)=\{y\in K:\mathrm{dist}(y,H)<\varepsilon\}. $$

Theorem 4 (Absence of sticking to hyperplanes and affine IPE). Let system 3 satisfy Assumption 2. Then there exists an invariant set  $ X_0 \subset K $ of full measure,  $ \mu(X_0) = 1 $, such that for every  $ x \in X_0 $ and every affine hyperplane  $ H \subset \mathbb{R}^n $ the fraction of time spent in the  $ \epsilon $-neighborhood of the hyperplane  $ U_\varepsilon(H) $ tends to zero:
$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{U_{\varepsilon}(H)}\big(\Phi^{t}x\big)dt=0. $$
Proof. The proof of the theorem is given in the Appendix. For simplicity of verification, a reference to a Lean formalization of this proof is also provided there.
Corollary 5. Consequently, for every  $ x \in X_0 $ the trajectory  $ t \mapsto \Phi^t(x) $ is affinely integrally exciting:
$$ \liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\phi_{z}(t)\phi_{z}(t)^{\top}dt>0. $$

As mentioned in the introduction, IPE for the state vector is considered mainly for clarity; the main theorems (the Birkhoff–Khinchin theorem [15, 16] and the Novikov–Yakovenko theorem [17]) used in the proof (see Appendix) allow one to generalize the result of the paper to an arbitrary polynomial regressor and to apply the theorem to the regressor that is used in a concrete work on parameter identification or adaptive control.
Let us now show how this theorem can be applied to a concrete model.
